passages.happening:
‘During the reign of David there was a famine for three successive years, and David sought the face of the LORD’ (verse 1). The LORD answers, “It is because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites” (verse 1).

The narrator explains. The Gibeonites were not Israelites but a remnant of the Amorites. Israel had sworn an oath to them, ‘but in his zeal for Israel and Judah, Saul had sought to kill them’ (verse 2).

David asks the Gibeonites, “What shall I do for you? How can I make amends so that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?” (verse 3). They want no silver or gold from Saul's house. They ask for seven of Saul's male descendants, to put them to death before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul. David agrees (verses 4-6).

He spares Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, because of his oath to Jonathan. He hands over two sons of Saul by his concubine Rizpah, and five grandsons of Saul through his daughter Merab. The Gibeonites put them to death on the hill before the LORD. ‘So all seven of them fell together; they were put to death in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 21 to 24 are a closing collection, not in the order of events. They gather stories, lists and poems from across David's reign. This one reaches back into the past. Saul has been dead for years, but a wrong he did still lies on the land. It probably belongs to the early or middle part of David's reign, after Mephibosheth came to his table, since verse 7 assumes that.

The Gibeonites lived in a cluster of towns north of Jerusalem, in Benjamin. In Joshua's day they tricked Israel into swearing a treaty of peace in the LORD's name, and Israel kept that oath even after the trick was found out. Saul's attempt to wipe them out is told nowhere else. This chapter is the only source, and it names his motive as zeal for Israel and Judah, perhaps a drive to clear non-Israelites out of Benjamin, his own tribe.

Israel took oaths sworn in the LORD's name with great seriousness. Breaking one invited judgment, and blood that was never answered was said to pollute the land. In that world famine was widely read as a sign of God's displeasure, and David does what a king should: he seeks the LORD. The verb behind make amends is the verb used for atonement in Israel's sacrifices. It shows how seriously the wrong was taken.

The Gibeonites refuse money and ask for a life-for-life settlement from the house of the man who tried to destroy them. The deaths take place at Gibeah, Saul's own town.
passages.later: Israel's leaders had said of the Gibeonites in Joshua's day, “We have sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we cannot touch them” (Joshua 9:19). The law warned, ‘for bloodshed pollutes the land’ (Numbers 35:33).
passages.hard:
How could God allow seven of Saul's descendants to die for Saul's crime?

This is one of the hardest passages in the historical books, and it should be read with its difficulty intact.

The text says that the LORD named the cause of the famine. It does not say that the LORD commanded the deaths. The Gibeonites asked for them, and David agreed. So some readers take the settlement as a human response within the customs of that time, which the narrator reports without approving every part of it. They point to the law itself: “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16).

Others argue that Saul's household was itself caught up in the massacre, since verse 1 speaks of the blood shed by Saul and his family, so that the men who died may not have been simply innocent. Still others note that the ancient world thought of guilt more as something a family or people shared than modern readers do. And some point out that the land was healed only after the burial, not straight after the deaths.

What the chapter plainly does is honor Rizpah, whose grief and faithfulness move the king, and it leaves the reader unsettled about the cost of broken oaths. The prophets would later insist that each person answers for his own sin. This story lays down no rule for today. It gives no family, church or state any right to punish one person for what another has done.
passages.asks: A promise made long ago, to a people Israel did not want to keep faith with, still mattered to God. Ask what promises you are tempted to treat as expired because the people you made them to do not count for much. And ask who still pays for a wrong done long ago by someone else.

passages.happening:
‘And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on a rock’ (verse 10). From the beginning of the harvest until the rain falls on the bodies, she does not let the birds touch them by day, or the wild animals by night.

When David is told what Rizpah has done, he goes and takes the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had taken them from the square at Beth-shan where the Philistines had hung them up. He has the bones of the seven gathered too. They bury the bones of Saul and Jonathan in the tomb of Saul's father Kish, in Benjamin (verses 11-14). ‘After they had done everything the king had commanded, God answered their prayers for the land’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
In that world, leaving a body unburied for birds and animals was the worst dishonor that could be done to the dead. Rizpah cannot save her sons, but she will not let them be shamed. She keeps watch on a rock, day and night, from the barley harvest in spring until the autumn rains. It is a mother's love and a mother's protest at once.

Rizpah appeared once before, named only as the cause of a quarrel between Ish-bosheth and Abner (3:7). Here she is given the chapter's noblest act.

Her faithfulness moves David, and the story turns from judgment to honor. He brings home the bones of Saul and Jonathan, who had lain at Jabesh since the men of that town rescued them after Gilboa, and gives them and the seven an honorable burial. Saul and Jonathan are laid in the family tomb in Benjamin. Only then does the narrator say that God answered prayer for the land. Saul's story comes to a quiet close: the first king and his son rest at last in Benjamin.
passages.later: The Psalms count unburied dead among the worst things that can happen to God's people: ‘They have given the corpses of Your servants as food to the birds of the air’ (Psalm 79:2), ‘and there is no one to bury the dead’ (Psalm 79:3).
passages.hard:
Did the deaths of the seven end the famine?

The text does not say so. It says that God answered prayer for the land after the bones had been buried, after Rizpah's vigil had moved the king to give the dead their honor. Some readers find that order important. The chapter's resolution comes after the dead of Saul's house were given their honor, not straight after the executions.

What the chapter shows with no uncertainty is Rizpah's grief. It is not hurried, and it is not rebuked. She could not change what happened, and her love still did what it could.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Rizpah could not stop what was done to her sons, but she would not let them be dishonored. Ask what faithful love can still do when it cannot change the outcome. And ask whose quiet vigil around you deserves to be noticed and honored.

passages.t: Giants, and the lamp of Israel
passages.happening:
Once again there is war with the Philistines. David goes down with his men and grows exhausted, and a descendant of Rapha named Ishbi-benob, with a heavy bronze spear and a new sword, means to kill him. Abishai comes to his aid and kills the Philistine. Then David's men swear to him, “You must never again go out with us to battle, so that the lamp of Israel may not be extinguished” (verse 17).

Three more battles follow. At Gob, Sibbecai kills Saph. At Gob again, ‘Elhanan son of Jair the Bethlehemite killed the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam’ (verse 19). And at Gath a huge man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot taunts Israel, and David's nephew Jonathan kills him. ‘So these four descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his servants’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The giants are called descendants of Rapha, linked with the Rephaim, a people Israel remembered as tall and formidable. The battles David once fought alone, as a young man against Goliath, are now fought by his servants.

David's men call him the lamp of Israel, the light whose going out would leave the nation in darkness. They will not risk him in battle again. The aging king has to be protected from his own limits.

Each of the four notes follows the same pattern: another battle, a named hero, a slain descendant of Rapha. The chapter as a whole is part of a careful design. It pairs with chapter 24: both open with a disaster on the land tied to a king's sin, and both end with God answering prayer for the land.
passages.later:
The same lamp is promised in Kings, where God keeps David's line burning in Jerusalem: ‘so that My servant David will always have a lamp before Me in Jerusalem’ (1 Kings 11:36).

Chronicles tells the same battles, with its own form of the names (1 Chronicles 20:4-8).
passages.hard:
Who killed Goliath? Verse 19 seems to give him to Elhanan.

The standard Hebrew of verse 19 says that Elhanan killed Goliath the Gittite, though 1 Samuel 17 gives Goliath to David. Chronicles says that Elhanan killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath (1 Chronicles 20:5). The BSB supplies the words the brother of from Chronicles.

Many scholars think the Samuel text was damaged in copying. The Hebrew word for weavers appears twice in the verse, in the name of Elhanan's father and in the weaver's beam, and Chronicles may keep the better reading. Others think Samuel keeps an older tradition that the Chronicler smoothed. Some suggest that Goliath was a name borne by more than one warrior. The site's page on the numbers in Samuel and Chronicles sets out all three, and these notes take no side.
passages.asks: David's men told him he could no longer go into battle. Ask when you have needed others to protect you from your own limits. And ask whether you are willing to let younger hands carry what you once carried alone.
